title: FMCSA Fuel-Hauler HOS Waiver: September 2026 | Hermes
description: FMCSA granted a temporary hours-of-service waiver for interstate motor carriers transporting gasoline and diesel fuel from September 16 through December 16, 2026. Hermes explains the scope, limits, and dispatch checks that matter before using it.
h1: FMCSA changed HOS limits for gasoline and diesel haulers. What should carriers verify before using the waiver?
conciseAnswer: FMCSA's September 16, 2026 waiver temporarily relaxes 49 CFR 395.3 for interstate motor carriers and drivers transporting gasoline and diesel fuel through December 16, 2026. It is not a blanket HOS exemption: eligibility, rest, recordkeeping, fatigue, safety-status, and crash-reporting conditions still apply.
explanation: What changed: FMCSA granted a temporary waiver from the property-carrying hours-of-service limits in 49 CFR 395.3 for interstate motor carriers and drivers transporting gasoline and diesel fuel. The waiver runs from September 16 through December 16, 2026. A driver using it may drive no more than 16 hours in any 24-hour period and must still meet the waiver's required rest conditions. The agency also requires the driver to carry a physical or digital copy of the waiver while operating under it.

Why it matters: this is targeted relief for fuel transportation, not a general extension for dry van, car hauling, reefer, flatbed, or other ordinary freight. Drivers subject to an out-of-service order are not eligible, and motor carriers with a conditional safety rating are excluded. Other applicable federal and state requirements remain in force, including CDL and endorsement rules, drug and alcohol testing, insurance, hazardous-material rules, and size and weight requirements.

What to do: before dispatching a movement under the waiver, confirm that the load actually qualifies as gasoline or diesel transportation, verify the driver's license and required endorsements, check that neither the driver nor carrier is disqualified by the waiver's safety-status restrictions, make the waiver available in the truck, and plan the required sleeper-berth or off-duty break. When moving back to normal operations, review the waiver's transition rule because a 10-hour break is required when qualifying waiver and normal operations reach the stated threshold.

Result: a carrier or dispatcher can use the temporary flexibility without treating it as a broad permission to extend every shift. The operational gain comes from matching the exact movement and driver to the waiver while preserving fatigue controls and the rest of the safety framework. Carriers using the waiver should also have a process for the FMCSA crash-notification requirement, which applies within two business days when a covered driver is involved in a reportable crash.

Hermes historical logistics material is used only as anonymized operating context: dispatch training repeatedly emphasized verifying the movement, route, timing, driver status, and approvals before acting. No historical rates, earnings, contacts, or private operational figures are used here, and the current compliance terms come from FMCSA's dated waiver rather than the archive.
takeaways: The waiver is effective September 16 through December 16, 2026 and is limited to interstate gasoline and diesel transportation
The 16-hour driving ceiling does not remove the waiver's rest, fatigue, eligibility, or safety-status conditions
Conditional-rated motor carriers and drivers or carriers under applicable out-of-service restrictions are not eligible
Use the FMCSA waiver itself as the compliance source; historical Hermes material is context only

faq.question: Does the waiver apply to every truckload carrier?
faq.answer: No. FMCSA limited this waiver to motor carriers and drivers transporting gasoline and diesel fuel in interstate commerce. Ordinary freight movements outside that scope do not gain the waiver's HOS flexibility.

faq.question: Can a qualifying driver simply work 16 hours without rest?
faq.answer: No. The waiver sets a 16-hour driving ceiling within a 24-hour period and separately requires specified consecutive sleeper-berth or off-duty rest. A driver who needs immediate rest must be allowed to stop and receive the required rest before resuming.

faq.question: Does the waiver replace CDL, hazmat, insurance, or drug-testing requirements?
faq.answer: No. FMCSA states that other applicable federal and state requirements remain in effect. The waiver is limited to specific HOS relief under 49 CFR 395.3.

faq.question: What should a dispatcher document before using the waiver?
faq.answer: At minimum, verify that the movement is covered fuel transportation, the driver has the required license and endorsements, the driver and carrier satisfy the waiver's eligibility rules, the required rest plan is workable, and a copy of the waiver is available to the driver.

title: Meta One Business Tools: What Teams Should Audit | Hermes
description: Meta introduced Meta One business and creator subscriptions with new publishing, analytics, team-access and AI features. Hermes Marketing explains what changed and how to evaluate the workflow impact before paying for another tool.
h1: Meta One adds new business publishing and analytics tools. What should a marketing team audit first?
conciseAnswer: Meta says its Meta One business and creator plans are rolling out with professional features inside Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. Availability varies by region, app and account, so teams should compare the live features in their own account against the tools and workflow they already pay for before changing their stack.
explanation: What changed: Meta announced Meta One on September 15, 2026. For business and creator plans, Meta describes professional tools that can include scheduling Stories up to 30 days ahead, adding links to organic posts and Reels, exportable analytics, deeper audience insights, team access without password sharing, and expanded Meta Business Agent capacity. Meta also says plan features and availability can vary by region, app, and account.

Why it matters: some work that previously required separate scheduling, reporting, access-management, or customer-response tools may now be available inside the Meta ecosystem. That can simplify an operating stack, but a new subscription does not replace content strategy, audience research, creative quality, conversion tracking, or a disciplined publishing cadence.

What to do: audit the exact features visible in the live business account before subscribing. List the scheduling, analytics, link, team-access, and response tools already in use; identify any duplicate cost; test whether the Meta-native feature actually removes a workflow bottleneck; and preserve a baseline for reach, clicks, leads, and conversion so any change can be measured rather than assumed.

Result: treat Meta One as a workflow decision, not a growth guarantee. A useful upgrade should reduce friction, improve access control, or make measurement easier. If the same capability already exists in the current stack, the team should keep the existing process until the new tool proves a measurable operational advantage.
takeaways: Meta One is rolling out business and creator tools across Meta apps, but availability varies by account and region
Advanced business features can include Story scheduling, organic links, exportable analytics, deeper audience insights, and team access without password sharing
Audit overlap with the current tool stack before adding another subscription
Measure workflow savings and business outcomes instead of assuming a platform feature will create growth

title: U.S. Diesel at $6.285/Gallon: Carrier Route Planning | Hermes
description: EIA reported U.S. on-highway diesel at $6.285 per gallon for September 14, 2026. Hermes connects the price shock to deadhead control, lane economics, and carrier rate decisions.
h1: U.S. diesel reached $6.285 per gallon. What changes for carrier route planning?
conciseAnswer: EIA reported the U.S. average on-highway diesel price at $6.285 per gallon for September 14, 2026, up $0.318 from the prior week. That does not create one universal rate target, but it makes empty miles, reload probability, route selection, timing, and fuel assumptions more important in every load decision.
explanation: Start with the current fact. The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported an average on-highway diesel price of $6.285 per gallon for September 14, 2026, compared with $5.967 one week earlier. The same table shows the national average $2.546 per gallon above the year-earlier level. For a carrier, that is not a reason to replace lane analysis with a single fuel headline. It is a reason to make fuel exposure explicit in the load decision instead of treating it as background noise.

Hermes historical dispatch material repeatedly treated route planning, deadhead reduction, broker negotiation, pickup and delivery verification, and the next reload as connected operating decisions. That older operating pattern becomes more important when diesel is expensive: an attractive loaded rate can still produce weak economics if the truck travels too far empty before pickup, lands in a weak reload area, waits through an inefficient appointment window, or must reposition again after delivery. The useful lesson from the archive is the decision sequence, not any old promised rate, commission, earnings level, or tool.

The practical response is to calculate the movement as a route, not as a headline rate. Before accepting or negotiating a load, separate loaded miles from deadhead to pickup and expected repositioning after delivery. Add the fuel assumption that fits the truck and route, then consider tolls, time, equipment fit, appointment risk, payment terms, and the quality of the likely next move. A national diesel average helps update the cost assumption; it does not decide whether a specific load works.

This also changes negotiation discipline. When fuel moves sharply in one week, stale internal assumptions can make yesterday's acceptable lane look different today. The carrier or dispatcher should be able to explain the operating reason behind a counteroffer—route, empty-mile exposure, timing, equipment or destination economics—rather than simply citing a national diesel number. That creates a more defensible conversation while avoiding claims that every broker, lane or customer must absorb the same adjustment.

The then-versus-now comparison is straightforward. Historical Hermes operating material already emphasized reducing deadhead and understanding where the truck can go next. The September 2026 EIA data raises the cost of getting those decisions wrong, but it does not change the underlying method: verify the lane, model the full movement, compare realistic alternatives, negotiate from the actual operating picture, and re-check assumptions when fuel or market conditions move.
takeaways: EIA put the U.S. on-highway diesel average at $6.285 per gallon for September 14, up $0.318 week over week
High diesel prices increase the importance of deadhead and reload planning; they do not create one universal carrier rate
Evaluate the full movement: loaded miles, empty miles, fuel, tolls, timing, equipment fit, payment terms and the likely next load
Hermes historical operating evidence supports the same core discipline—route planning and deadhead control—but old commercial claims are not reused as current truth

faq.question: Does $6.285 diesel mean every load rate should rise by the same amount?
faq.answer: No. The EIA figure is a national fuel-price benchmark, not a lane-specific rate instruction. The effect on a load depends on the truck, miles, deadhead, route, timing, equipment, tolls, reload options and other operating costs.

faq.question: Why does deadhead matter more when fuel is expensive?
faq.answer: Empty miles still consume fuel and time without producing loaded revenue. When the fuel assumption rises, unnecessary positioning and weak reload planning can have a larger effect on the economics of the full trip.

faq.question: Should a carrier use the national diesel price as its only fuel input?
faq.answer: No. The national average is useful context. A carrier should use a fuel assumption that reflects the actual truck, route and operating conditions when calculating a specific movement.

faq.answer: The archive shows that Hermes dispatch training and operations historically treated route planning, deadhead reduction, load fit and negotiation as connected decisions. It is used here only as anonymized operating context; old rates, commissions, earnings claims and private details are not treated as current facts.

title: Dry Van Spot Rates: $2.21/Mile Carrier Analysis | Hermes
description: DAT reported dry-van spot linehaul averaging $2.21 per mile for the week ending September 4, 2026. Hermes explains how carriers should use that market average without treating it as a guaranteed lane rate.
h1: Dry van spot rates rose to $2.21 per mile. What should carriers do with that information?
conciseAnswer: DAT reported U.S. dry-van spot linehaul averaging $2.21 per mile for the week ending September 4, 2026, excluding fuel. That is useful market context, not a universal booking target. A carrier still needs to compare the specific lane, loaded miles, deadhead, fuel, tolls, equipment fit, payment terms, timing, and the likely next move before deciding whether a load works.
explanation: Start with what the DAT number actually represents. The $2.21 figure is an average spot linehaul rate paid to carriers and excludes fuel. DAT reported it up 1.1% week over week and 33.6% year over year. That tells a carrier the market was materially firmer than a year earlier, but it does not tell you what one broker, lane, pickup window, destination, or piece of equipment should pay.

Capacity matters because the same rate can mean something different as trucks return. DAT reported load posts down 0.9% week over week while truck posts rose 1.4%, which moved the load-to-truck ratio down to 11.47 from 11.73. The ratio was still far above 6.68 a year earlier, so the market remained comparatively tight even as capacity started to loosen. For negotiation, that supports using current conditions as leverage without assuming the strongest week will continue unchanged.

Regional averages also show why a national number cannot be used as a lane quote. DAT listed Ohio River and Great Lakes at $2.67 per mile, Southeast at $2.29, Carolinas at $2.26, and Florida–South Georgia at $1.51 for the week. A carrier moving into a weaker destination can accept a respectable outbound rate and still damage the round-trip economics if the return lane, reload timing, or deadhead is poor.

Turn the market report into a load decision by calculating an internal floor before the call. Start with the revenue offered for the load, then subtract the costs and empty-mile exposure that actually belong to that movement. A practical worksheet should include loaded miles, deadhead to pickup, expected deadhead after delivery, fuel, tolls, variable operating cost, time requirements, payment terms, and any equipment or access constraint. The market average is then a comparison point, not the calculation itself.

DAT's 35-day forecast placed dry-van spot linehaul near $2.20 per mile in mid-October with an uncertainty band around plus or minus $0.08. Forecasts are useful for planning conversations and setting review dates, but they are not guarantees. Hermes would use that forecast to decide when to re-check lane floors and negotiation assumptions, not to promise a future rate, utilization level, or revenue outcome.
takeaways: $2.21 per mile was linehaul only; fuel was excluded
Truck supply rose faster than load posts, so the load-to-truck ratio eased to 11.47
Regional averages ranged widely, making lane context more important than a national average
Use market data to challenge assumptions, then calculate the actual load with deadhead and operating cost

faq.question: Does a $2.21 national average mean a carrier should reject every dry-van load below $2.21 per mile?
faq.answer: No. A national average is market context, not a universal floor. The correct decision depends on the specific lane, deadhead, fuel, tolls, equipment, timing, payment terms, operating costs, and what the truck can do after delivery.

faq.question: Did the DAT rate include fuel?
faq.answer: No. DAT states that the cited dry-van spot linehaul rates exclude fuel costs and surcharges unless otherwise noted.

faq.question: Why can a strong outbound rate still be a weak load?
faq.answer: The return lane can change the economics. Long deadhead after delivery, weak reload demand, appointment delays, tolls, or equipment constraints can offset a strong outbound price.

faq.question: Does the market forecast guarantee that rates will stay near $2.20 per mile?
faq.answer: No. DAT publishes a forecast with an uncertainty range. It is planning context, not a guaranteed future rate, load volume, utilization level, or carrier revenue.
